subject: Economy
sub_topic: Repo rate and reverse repo rate

concepts.name: Repo Rate: Definition, Mechanism and Collateral Framework
key_dimensions: Precise definition: rate at which RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities
Role of collateral — eligible securities under LAF (G-Secs, T-Bills, State Development Loans)
Repurchase agreement structure: banks sell securities and agree to buy back at a higher price
UPSC trap: Repo is NOT a simple loan — it is a collateralised borrowing with a repurchase obligation

concepts.name: Reverse Repo Rate: Definition and Directional Logic
key_dimensions: Rate at which RBI borrows money FROM commercial banks (absorbs excess liquidity)
Directional trap: always LOWER than repo rate — forms the floor of the LAF corridor
Banks park surplus funds with RBI overnight at reverse repo rate
UPSC trap: Reverse repo is RBI's tool to ABSORB liquidity, not inject it — opposite of repo

concepts.name: Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF): The Operational Framework
key_dimensions: LAF is the corridor within which repo and reverse repo operate — introduced in 2000 post Narasimham Committee
Components: Repo (injection), Reverse Repo (absorption), and Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)
The interest rate corridor: MSF Rate > Repo Rate > Reverse Repo Rate
UPSC trap: LAF is an operating procedure, not a standalone rate — repo/reverse repo are instruments within LAF

concepts.name: Policy Repo Rate as the Benchmark: Signal vs. Operational Rate
key_dimensions: Post-2014 Urjit Patel Committee: Policy repo rate made the single operating target of monetary policy
Distinction between 'policy rate' (signalling) and 'operating rate' (actual market rate RBI targets)
Weighted Average Call Rate (WACR) is the operational target — RBI tries to anchor it near repo rate
UPSC trap: Repo rate is the POLICY rate, but the actual operating target is WACR, not repo rate itself

concepts.name: Transmission Mechanism: How Repo Rate Changes Affect the Economy
key_dimensions: Transmission chain: Repo Rate → Bank lending rates (MCLR/EBLR) → Credit demand → Investment → Output & Inflation
Asymmetric transmission problem: banks pass on rate hikes faster than rate cuts
External Benchmark Lending Rate (EBLR) introduced in 2019 to improve transmission — directly linked to repo rate
UPSC trap: Change in repo rate does NOT automatically change deposit/lending rates — transmission is imperfect and lagged

concepts.name: Repo Rate and Inflation Control: Contractionary Monetary Policy
key_dimensions: Raising repo rate → increases cost of borrowing → reduces money supply → controls demand-pull inflation
Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) framework: RBI mandated to keep CPI inflation at 4% ±2%
UPSC trap: Repo rate is effective against demand-pull inflation, NOT cost-push (supply-side) inflation
Conflict between inflation control and growth — raising repo rate may hurt GDP growth simultaneously

concepts.name: Repo Rate and Economic Growth: Accommodative vs. Restrictive Stance
key_dimensions: Lowering repo rate → cheaper credit → increased investment and consumption → economic stimulus
Monetary policy stance terminology: Accommodative (rate cuts likely), Neutral, Calibrated Tightening, Withdrawal of Accommodation
UPSC trap: 'Withdrawal of accommodation' does NOT mean rate hike — it means the next move is unlikely to be a cut
Tension between growth and inflation mandates, especially during stagflation scenarios

concepts.name: Marginal Standing Facility (MSF): The Emergency Borrowing Window
key_dimensions: MSF rate = Repo Rate + 25 bps (typically) — banks can borrow overnight beyond their normal LAF quota
Banks can borrow against SLR securities — can even dip into SLR holdings (up to a limit) to borrow under MSF
MSF forms the CEILING of the LAF interest rate corridor
UPSC trap: MSF rate is always HIGHER than repo rate; it is a penal/emergency rate, not the standard borrowing rate

concepts.name: The Interest Rate Corridor: Floor, Ceiling and Width
key_dimensions: Floor = Reverse Repo Rate (currently Repo - 25 bps post-2020 SDF introduction, or Standing Deposit Facility)
Ceiling = MSF Rate (Repo + 25 bps)
Width of corridor = 50 bps (25 bps on each side of repo rate in normal times)
UPSC trap: After introduction of SDF in April 2022, SDF rate replaced reverse repo as the effective floor — SDF rate = Repo - 25 bps

concepts.name: Standing Deposit Facility (SDF): New Floor of LAF Corridor
key_dimensions: Introduced in April 2022 Budget — RBI absorbs excess liquidity WITHOUT giving collateral to banks
SDF rate = Repo Rate - 25 bps (currently) — it is the new effective floor of the LAF corridor
Key difference from reverse repo: SDF is uncollateralised (RBI does not provide G-Secs in return)
UPSC trap: After SDF introduction, reverse repo rate became less relevant operationally — SDF is the new floor, NOT reverse repo

concepts.name: Monetary Policy Committee (MPC): Who Decides the Repo Rate
key_dimensions: MPC constituted under amended RBI Act Section 45ZB — 6 members: 3 RBI officials + 3 government nominees
Decisions by majority vote; RBI Governor has casting vote in case of tie
MPC decides ONLY the policy repo rate — operational decisions (like CRR, SLR) remain with RBI Board
UPSC trap: MPC does NOT decide reverse repo rate independently — it is set as a spread below repo rate by RBI

concepts.name: Repo Rate vs. Bank Rate: Key Distinctions
key_dimensions: Bank Rate: rate at which RBI provides long-term credit — no collateral requirement, no repurchase agreement
Repo Rate: short-term (usually overnight), collateralised, with repurchase obligation
Post-LAF: Bank Rate = MSF Rate (aligned since 2012) — used mainly as penal rate for SLR defaults
UPSC trap: Bank Rate and Repo Rate are NOT the same — Bank Rate is for long-term lending, repo is short-term and collateralised

concepts.name: CRR and SLR: Distinction from Repo and Reverse Repo as Liquidity Tools
key_dimensions: CRR/SLR are quantity-based tools (control money supply directly); Repo/Reverse Repo are price-based tools (control cost of money)
CRR change has immediate and powerful effect; Repo rate change works through transmission mechanism (indirect)
UPSC trap: RBI can control liquidity via BOTH quantity tools (CRR) and price tools (repo) — they are complements, not substitutes
Reducing CRR injects permanent liquidity; repo injection is temporary (overnight or short-term)

concepts.name: Repo Rate Impact on Exchange Rate and Capital Flows
key_dimensions: Higher repo rate → higher domestic interest rates → attracts foreign capital (FPI debt inflows) → rupee appreciation
Lower repo rate → capital outflows risk → rupee depreciation pressure
Interest rate differential between India and US Fed rate influences carry trade and rupee stability
UPSC trap: RBI faces a trilemma — cannot simultaneously have independent monetary policy, fixed exchange rate, and free capital flows

concepts.name: Real Repo Rate vs. Nominal Repo Rate
key_dimensions: Real Repo Rate = Nominal Repo Rate − Inflation Rate (CPI); negative real rates stimulate, positive real rates tighten
RBI targets positive real interest rates to maintain credibility under FIT framework
During COVID, real repo rate was negative — deliberate accommodative stance
UPSC trap: A LOWER nominal repo rate during HIGH inflation can still be contractionary in real terms if real rate rises

concepts.name: Open Market Operations (OMO) vs. Repo: Complementary Liquidity Tools
key_dimensions: OMO: RBI buys/sells G-Secs in open market — permanent liquidity injection/absorption; changes bank reserves
Repo: temporary liquidity management — reversed at maturity; does not permanently alter money supply
Variable Rate Repo (VRR) vs. Fixed Rate Repo — VRR allows market-determined rates for longer tenors
UPSC trap: OMO purchase injects PERMANENT liquidity while repo injection is TEMPORARY — both involve G-Secs but differ in permanence

concepts.name: Repo Rate and Asset Price Inflation: Beyond CPI Targeting
key_dimensions: Low repo rates can fuel asset price bubbles (real estate, stock markets) even when CPI remains controlled
RBI's mandate targets CPI, NOT asset prices — creates a policy blind spot
Macroprudential tools (LTV ratios, sectoral risk weights) used alongside repo rate to address asset bubbles
UPSC trap: RBI does NOT target stock market or housing prices via repo rate — this is a deliberate limitation of inflation targeting

concepts.name: Repo Rate Changes: Frequency, Quantum and Forward Guidance
key_dimensions: MPC meets bi-monthly (6 times a year) — rate changes typically in multiples of 25 bps
Forward guidance: RBI communicates future stance to manage market expectations (e.g., 'stance remains accommodative')
Surprise rate changes outside scheduled MPC meetings possible in emergency (e.g., COVID May 2020 off-cycle cut)
UPSC trap: Stance change and rate change are DIFFERENT signals — stance can change without a rate change (e.g., neutral stance with unchanged repo rate)

concepts.name: Historical Context: Repo and Reverse Repo Rate Trends and Crisis Response
key_dimensions: Post-GFC 2008: RBI cut repo rate sharply — repo from 9% to 4.75% (2009) to stimulate economy
COVID-19 response: Repo cut to historic low of 4% (May 2020); reverse repo cut more aggressively to 3.35% to discourage parking
UPSC trap: During COVID, RBI widened the LAF corridor asymmetrically by cutting reverse repo MORE than repo — deliberate to force banks to lend rather than park funds
2022–2023 rate hike cycle: Repo raised from 4% to 6.5% in response to post-COVID inflation surge

concepts.name: Reverse Repo Rate Asymmetric Cut: COVID-Era Policy Innovation
key_dimensions: RBI cut reverse repo rate by 90 bps vs. 40 bps for repo during COVID — widened corridor from 25 bps to 65 bps
Rationale: Discourage banks from parking excess liquidity with RBI; nudge them to lend to productive sectors
This created a 'disincentive' mechanism — banks earned less by parking with RBI than by lending
UPSC trap: Asymmetric corridor is NOT a standard feature — it was an emergency innovation; understanding WHY it was done is key
